```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set( collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>" )
library(pfmatch)
tab <- function(d, ...) knitr::kable(d, format = "html", ...)
```

```{r data, echo = FALSE}
# Measured, not illustrative. Every figure on this page comes from
# inputs/ef100k_grants.csv (100,000 grant rows) scored against the filed
# recipient-status field, except where the text says otherwise. Embedded as
# literals so the vignette builds without the inputs directory, which is not
# shipped in the package.
rule_tbl <- data.frame(
  rule = c("filed status code alone",
           "202-name given-name whitelist (removed)",
           "two tokens both in `census.names`",
           "`org_score < 0.05`, no token constraint",
           "**`org_score < 0.05` on a 2-3 token name**"),
  recall = c("100% by construction", "30.7%", "49.4%", "76.0%", "**73.6%**"),
  fp     = c("—", "0.9%", "2.0%", "0.5%", "**0.4%**"),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(rule_tbl) <- c("How the recipient is judged a person",
                     "Caught, of 3,211 declared individuals",
                     "Fired, of 71,762 declared charities")

flag_tbl <- data.frame(
  flag = c("`flag_individual`", "`flag_government`",
           "`looks_personal`", "`flag_placeholder`"),
  source = c("the filed status field", "the filed status field",
             "the recipient name", "the recipient name"),
  what = c("the filer coded this payee `I` / `INDIVIDUAL`",
           "the filer coded it a government body",
           "the name reads as a natural person",
           "the name is a pointer to an attachment, not a name"),
  n = c("3,211", "783", "5,209", "283"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(flag_tbl) <- c("Flag", "Read from", "Means", "Rows per 100k")

ph_tbl <- data.frame(
  detector = c("`pf_placeholder_pattern()` alone",
               "peopleparser `placeholder` class alone",
               "**the union, which is what fires**"),
  rows = c("272", "147", "**283**"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(ph_tbl) <- c("Detector", "Rows caught per 100k")
```

A 990-PF filer reports who it paid, and some of those payees are people:
scholarship and fellowship recipients, prize winners, hardship grants. A person
has no EIN and no Business Master File record, so a person routed into the
matching cascade can only do one of two things — fail, or match an organisation
that happens to share a surname. Both are wrong, and the first is worse than it
looks, because it is counted as a match failure.

This is a **denominator** problem rather than a matching problem. Individuals
sitting in the population make every clear rate in the project read low, and
the error does not get smaller as matching improves. Identifying them is
therefore worth doing carefully, and worth measuring rather than assuming.

## The four flags

`pf_prepare_grants()` attaches four flags to every row. Two are what the filer
*said*; two are read off the name itself.

```{r flags, echo = FALSE}
tab( flag_tbl )
```

All four are flags, not filters. None of them removes a row from the matching
population — `in_scope` is decided by geography and by whether there is
anything to match on at all. That separation is deliberate: the filed status
field is wrong often enough in both directions that letting it decide scope
would silently discard real organisations.

## What the filed status field is worth

`SIGOCPYRFSTA` is uncontrolled text, and filers use it loosely. It is still the
single strongest signal available — a filer who writes `I` usually does mean an
individual — but it cannot be trusted alone, in either direction:

* Of 100 hand-adjudicated recipients in the residual (`dev/NO-RESIDUAL-AUDIT.md`),
  the pipeline's own signals flagged **28** as individual payees. Adjudication
  put the true count at **37**.
* The same audit found seven payees that are not organisations at all
  affirmatively coded `public_charity`.
* An earlier audit found the out-of-scope flag wrong **24%** of the time in the
  opposite sense, coding real organisations as individuals.

So the name has to be read as well. Everything below is about doing that.

## Reading the name

The name signal comes from `peopleparser::classify_names()`, whose model scores
each token on how much more often it appears in organisation names than in
people's names, combines that with token count and with given-name and surname
hits in the 2020 Census name lists, and was trained on Form 990 Part VII names
from 2009 to 2025 — 982,000 filer names against 9.4 million person names.

```{r classify}
x <- c( "BETH SMITH",
        "JONES MAURICE",
        "HARLEM CHILDRENS ZONE",
        "ASPCA",
        "BARNARD COLLEGE",
        "SEE ATTACHED SCHEDULE" )

peopleparser::classify_names( x ) |> tab()
```

### Read `org_score`, never `name_type`

This is the trap, and it is worth stating plainly because the column that looks
right is the wrong one. `classify_names()` only *labels* a name an organisation
once its score clears **0.99** for one- and two-word names — a threshold tuned
for officer lists, where most two-word entries really are people. Grant
recipient fields are full of acronyms and short institutional names, so the
label is far too generous:

```{r trap}
x <- c( "ASPCA", "KQED", "BARNARD COLLEGE", "CHARITY NAVIGATOR", "SMITH COLLEGE" )

# every one of these is an organisation, and every one is labelled "person"
peopleparser::classify_names( x ) |> tab()
```

On the 100,000-row file, **5,264 of the 13,348 rows labelled `person` score
above 0.8**. Taking the label at face value fires on 7.7% of filer-declared
public charities. Reading the score at 0.05 fires on 0.4%. Same model, same
call, twenty-fold difference in precision — the whole of it in which column you
read.

### Why a token count is still needed

The score alone is not enough. A one-token recipient is never a person's full
name, but the model will happily score a bare surname or an unfamiliar acronym
as person-like: `FRICK`, `CHIP`, `CISA`, `MARC`, `CHOW`. Requiring **2 to 3
tokens**, which the rule this replaced also did, costs 2.3 points of recall and
removes that whole class. On the shipped `pf_variants` corpus it cuts false
positives from 39 names to 16.

### How the rules compare

Measured against the filed status on 100,000 rows. Recall is the share of
declared individuals caught; the last column is the share of declared public
charities the rule fires on, which is the cost side.

```{r rules, echo = FALSE}
tab( rule_tbl )
```

The shipped rule is the last row. Two things to note. The whitelist it replaced
was not merely beaten — it was beaten on **both** axes at once, more than
double the recall for less than half the false-positive rate, which is why
there was no trade-off to debate. And the two-token census-match rule, the
obvious thing to build by hand from the same Census tables, is worse than
either: matching a given name against a surname is one of the inputs the model
already weighs, and weighing it alone over-fires on names like `GUILD HALL`.

### What it still misses

Of the seven people the old whitelist was documented to miss, six now flag.
`BROOKLYN GARRISON-OSBORN` scores 0.115 and still does not. A 0.25 cutoff
catches it, and also drags in `RONALD MCDONALD HOUSE`, `DANA FARBER` and
`Y M C A`, so 0.05 is where the cutoff sits.

## Placeholders: the third kind of recipient

Some filers decline to itemize Part XIV Table 3a and file one row whose
recipient name is a pointer — `SEE ATTACHED SCHEDULE`, `VARIOUS`,
`AVAILABLE UPON REQUEST` — carrying the whole year's total. There is no
recipient to find, on paper or anywhere else; see `vignette("outside-the-bmf")`
and `pf_attached_report()`.

These matter here for two reasons.

**First, they look like people.** `SEE ATTACHED` is two tokens with no
institutional word in it, which is exactly the shape the person score rewards.
Before `flag_placeholder` existed, 99 rows per 100k were flagged as natural
persons, every one of them a `SEE ...` variant. A placeholder now always wins:

```{r precedence}
x <- c( "SEE ATTACHED", "SEE SCHEDULE ATTACHED", "BETH SMITH" )

pf_is_placeholder( data.frame(recip_name = x) )
```

**Second, neither detector finds them all.** `pf_placeholder_pattern()` is a
hand-written regular expression, and peopleparser has its own `placeholder`
class. They disagree in both directions, so the flag is their union:

```{r ph, echo = FALSE}
tab( ph_tbl )
```

The pattern keeps the larger share, because it was written against this corpus.
What the model adds is the shapes a keyword list did not anticipate — the
`ALL OTHER(S) ...` family (`ALL OTHERS 1000 OR LESS PER DONEE`,
`ALL OTHER MEDICAL MISSIONS`), `THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES`, and bare `SEE` and `X`.

```{r pattern}
pf_placeholder_pattern()
```

Together they account for 283 rows per 100k across 166 distinct names, carrying
**4.0% of all grant dollars** in the file — $201.8M of $5.06B. That is the
reason this is a flag and not a filter: those dollars should be visible in a
report, not silently dropped from the population.

### Two defects this surfaced

Writing the flag turned up two problems in the pattern that had been there all
along.

`^MISC` matched `MISCARRIAGE ABORTION HOTLINE`, a real organisation with an
EIN, and discarded it as a pointer. The fix is two branches rather than one,
because `^MISC\b` alone would drop `MISCELLEANOUS` — a filer's misspelling that
is a genuine pointer.

The pattern also over-reaches on a named recipient with a pointer appended:
`WEILL CORNELL MEDICAL COLLEGE- SEE ATTACHMENT` and
`COLLEGE OF WESTERN IDAHO - SEE ADDENDUM FOR A` are both matchable
organisations whose names are right there. This one is **not fixed**. It costs
nothing while the flag is diagnostic, and it is the strongest argument against
promoting placeholders to a scope exclusion without first separating "a pointer
instead of a name" from "a name with a pointer stuck to it".

## Caveats worth carrying

**The labels are the filed status field, which is itself unreliable.** Both
populations are noisy, and in both directions, so the 0.4% is an *upper* bound
on the true false-positive rate. The declared-charity rows that the person flag
fires on include genuine filer miscodes — `JOEL OSTEEN`, `VIOLA WATSON`,
`PHELPS MICHAEL` — alongside genuine model errors — `MSPCA-ANGELL`,
`CHOATE ROSEMARY HALL`, `826 VALENCIA`. A clean read of precision needs hand
adjudication on a fresh stratified sample, which has not been done.

**The model was trained on filer and officer names, not grant recipients.** It
transfers well, but it was not fitted to this population, and the 0.99 default
threshold is direct evidence of that mismatch.

**The irreducible shape is the short two-token institutional name.**
`BETH ISRAEL` is a top-200 given name beside a census surname; `MECHON HADAR`,
`KEREN EZRA`, `SHAARE BINA` and `YISMACH MOSHE` are the same problem. No
name-only rule separates these from people, and 16 of them are allowlisted by
name in the package's own tests so that a genuinely personal name entering the
shipped corpus still trips the privacy guard there.

**Nicknames do not help.** peopleparser also ships `first_name_pairs`, 24,967
nickname and spelling-variant pairs. It is a within-person canonicalisation
table — both forms of a name are person names either way — so it contributes
nothing to telling people from organisations. Its use is on the matching side.

**The denominator has moved.** Every clear rate computed before this flag
changed was computed on the old one. Re-run before re-quoting.
